A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BaxBench study and contain readable main text and Appendices A-D. Methods, equations, tables, figures and prompt examples can be matched across the reformatting, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original evaluations of 11 LLMs on 392 backend-generation tasks, including correctness, security and prompting analyses.

after.justification: The original benchmark evaluations remain, with additional OpenHands results, a Snyk Code comparison and manual analysis of unsuccessful generated programs.

M1.justification: The core benchmark procedure remains scenario-plus-framework generation followed by Docker-based functional tests and security exploits. The prompt templates and calculator implementation examples are retained. OpenHands is an additional evaluated system, without a redesign of the proposed benchmark method.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same 28 backend scenarios, 14 frameworks, six languages, 54 endpoints and 13 CWE categories. The additional experiments use existing tasks or generated programs; changed specification lengths do not establish different task requirements or expanded coverage.

E2.justification: The eleven-model roster remains, but v3 adds Claude-3.5 Sonnet with OpenHands as a comparator against the base model in Table 2. Snyk Code, previously used during exploit construction, becomes an explicitly evaluated comparator against BaxBench exploits. These introduce agent and security-analyzer comparison settings.

E3.justification: New protocols include an OpenHands comparison on 351 tasks excluding Python-Django and Compiler, a Snyk evaluation of 237 correct o1 programs with manual adjudication, and inspection of 20 incorrect o1 programs. These substantially extend the evaluation design while retaining the main benchmark's metrics and sampling settings.

E4.justification: V3 adds analyses of whether agent scaffolding improves generation, whether independently detected vulnerabilities escape the exploits, and why o1 programs fail. The coverage study identifies 64 vulnerable programs missed by Snyk and seven additional valid flags missed by the exploits. Existing prompting, framework, complexity and calculator analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten samples per task for non-reasoning models and one for reasoning models, using the same pass@k estimator in Appendix D.1. Neither adds seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or other uncertainty reporting. New study sample sizes concern evaluation design.

E6.justification: Figure 3 revises o1 correctness from 60% to 62% and o3-mini secure correctness from 35% to 37%; DeepSeek-R1 overtakes Claude-3.5 Sonnet. Unsubscribe's no-reminder CWE-863 rate changes from 0.68 to 0.05 in v1 Table 5 versus v3 Table 6. Specification-length statistics, OpenAPI comparisons, complexity findings and appendix scores also change, alongside new agent and validation outcomes. These are revised reports, not established improvements under identical inputs and testing.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 retains the same pass@k estimator, sec_pass@k definition and security upper-bound reasoning. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract changes the exploitable fraction from 'more than half' to 'around half', and the introduction extends the insufficient-performance claim to LLM agents. The central benchmark contribution, three contribution bullets and deployment-readiness conclusion retain their meaning.

C2.justification: The new Discussion connects failures to boilerplate and API-compliance weaknesses, hypothesizes an excessive training emphasis on algorithmic coding, and recommends targeted data and post-training. V3 also interprets agent results through repository-context advantages, emphasizes test-time compute, and discusses contamination and withholding golden solutions. These substantially extend v1's interpretations and qualifications.

D1.justification: V3 documents OpenHands sandbox incompatibilities and task exclusions, explicitly advertises leaderboard access, changes planned-release wording to a release statement, and discloses that golden solutions are withheld. Existing package versions, Docker descriptions and Appendix C prompt templates are substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds OpenHands, SWE-Lancer and ProSec references and removes He and Vechev's 2023 security-hardening reference. These support the new agent comparison and training discussion, while the central positioning against function-level and repository-context benchmarks remains. Publication updates to retained references are bibliographic changes.

P1.justification: V3 streamlines passages, adds a Discussion before Related Work and an Impact Statement, and updates author and publication text. The main narrative progression and Appendices A-D remain substantially intact; most retained material receives local editing rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The main text switches to a two-column conference layout. V3 adds the agent table, relocates and resizes numerous displays, enlarges most appendix scenario plots onto individual pages, and changes plotted category ordering and some axes. This is extensive visual reorganization beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens an already extensive benchmark study with direct exploit-coverage validation, an agent comparison and useful failure and contamination discussion. These improve empirical grounding and interpretation. However, the relationship between changed specification statistics and revised scores remains unexplained, and Figure 3's caption still reports 35% despite its 37% bar. The benefits support a limited net quality improvement.
